title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Dowagiac neighbors sue over nonstop data center noise, seeking buyouts amid statewide siting fights.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Monday, July 27, and we're starting with a story hitting close to home for folks in southwest Michigan.
That's right — today we're talking about the Dowagiac data center where residents say the constant hum is driving them to sue for buyouts.
Exactly. Neighbors describe it like a vacuum running nonstop, violating local noise rules. The company was already fined and is now offering to buy affected homes.
Graham, walk me through why this feels like more than just one noisy facility.
Well, data centers need massive cooling systems, and those fans create low-frequency hums that travel far, especially in quiet rural spots like Dowagiac.
So how long has this been building? Have we seen similar complaints before in Michigan?
This isn't brand new — cooling noise has popped up around other projects, but Dowagiac is the first where it's escalated to buyout offers after a fine.
Who are the main players here? The company, the township, the residents?
Residents are leading the push with complaints and now legal action. The operator has tried fines and buyouts to quiet things down, while local officials enforce the noise ordinances.
What does this mean for people's daily lives — sleep, property values, that sort of thing?
Folks report disrupted sleep and constant background noise that makes normal living tough. Nearby homes could see values drop if the issue spreads.
And how does this tie into the bigger picture of water use and farmland we've heard about?
Data centers pull huge amounts of water for cooling and take up land that was often farmland. Noise is just the latest quality-of-life hit on top of those pressures.
Graham, what happens next if more projects skip stronger sound rules?
Other Michigan towns could face the same lawsuits or demands for buyouts. It might push counties to add noise limits when they review applications.
Any sense of how widespread these noise rules are right now?
Most places rely on general ordinances, but after cases like this, we're seeing more townships draft specific decibel or setback requirements for cooling equipment.
Does the buyout offer change the dynamic for residents who want to stay?
It gives some an exit, but others worry it sets a precedent where companies just pay to expand rather than fix the noise at the source.
And for the utility side, does this affect power demand or rates at all?
Not directly, but every new facility adds load that ties back to the rate debates we've seen elsewhere this week.
Fair point. So what's the takeaway for listeners in other rural counties?
Pay attention to how your township handles noise standards now — it could determine whether you end up with the same hum outside your window.
Alright, let's shift to the rest of the week's developments. Yesterday Chippewa County started weighing a temporary moratorium on new data centers.
Right — leaders there want time to study land, power, and service impacts before more proposals come in.
That could stall things in the eastern Upper Peninsula if it passes.
Exactly, and it shows how rural counties are reacting as interest grows.
On Saturday, Senate candidates laid out different ideas on regulating data-center power demand and protecting ratepayers from transmission costs.
Yes, the exchange highlighted real differences on whether utilities or tech firms should cover upgrades or if costs spread to everyone.
Primary voters now have clear contrasts on an issue that hits monthly bills.
Also Saturday, Indiana Michigan Power pledged that residential customers won't pay for new data-center power lines in their southwest Michigan territory.
That's a direct response to concerns about AI-driven demand pushing up bills.
Consumer groups are watching to see how it holds in future rate cases.
Moving to Friday, Garfield Township blocked new data centers for at least a year after an incomplete application.
Residents there now have breathing room to address power lines, water, and property values.
The pause lets them write rules before anything locks in.
DTE's Q2 preview that same day flagged data-center growth as a key earnings driver.
Which often means more grid demand and potential costs passed to households.
Calhoun County commissioners are also debating a year-long halt over electricity strain and whether jobs will benefit local taxpayers.
A pause would delay projects drawing hundreds of megawatts and millions of gallons of water.
Augusta Township is nearing a vote on zoning and tax terms for a large proposal pulling from the same DTE area as Saline.
The outcome will shape how much new load hits ratepayers and what revenue the township sees.
On Thursday we heard more from Dowagiac residents about ongoing noise and legal options, including possible class-action steps.
That lines up with today's buyout news.
Also Thursday, Saline Township reversed an earlier limit and restored Oracle's shot at a big tax break.
After company lobbying, residents now face forgoing years of property-tax revenue on a multibillion-dollar project.
Supporters point to jobs, but the power and water draw remains a concern.
No major public meetings listed for today on our tracker.
We'll keep watching township boards for any last-minute agendas.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Dowagiac Noise Battle: Residents Push for Buyouts as Data Center Hum Disrupts Lives
